sections.heading: Jainism and Buddhism — the heterodox reaction

blocks.text: The 6th century BCE saw a wave of **shramana (renouncer) movements** reacting against Vedic ritualism, Brahmanical dominance, sacrificial expense (cattle-killing hurt the agrarian economy) and caste rigidity — riding the urbanising, mercantile Mahajanapada society (the vaishya trading class patronised faiths that dignified their status). The two that endured: **Jainism** (**Vardhamana Mahavira**, the 24th and last **Tirthankara** — Parshvanatha the 23rd was historical) and **Buddhism** (**Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha — 'the enlightened one'**).

rows: Mahavira; **extreme ahimsa, asceticism**; the world is eternal (no creator god)
**Triratna** (right faith-knowledge-conduct); **anekantavada** (many-sidedness), **syadvada**; **5 vows** (ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha, brahmacharya)
**Four Noble Truths** (suffering, its cause-desire, cessation, path), **Eightfold Path**, anatta (no-soul), anicca (impermanence), nirvana
Liberation (kaivalya) via severe austerity, even **sallekhana** (fasting to death)
Nirvana via ethical-mental discipline; the Middle Way
Pali; spread across Asia (the first world religion from India)

items: **Councils & canon**: Buddhist councils — 1st (Rajagriha), 2nd (Vaishali — the schism), **3rd (Pataliputra, Ashoka — Tripitaka finalised), 4th (Kashmir, Kanishka — Mahayana emerges)**; the **Tripitaka (Sutta-Vinaya-Abhidhamma)**; Jain council at **Pataliputra then Vallabhi (Agamas canonised)**.

**Historical impact**: challenged caste and ritual, dignified non-violence (ahimsa's deep imprint on Indian civilisation → Gandhi), advanced **Prakrit-Pali vernaculars and trade** (merchants funded viharas along routes), and produced **art (stupas-Sanchi-Bharhut, cave-Ajanta-Ellora) and universities (Nalanda-Vikramshila)**; Buddhism became a world religion, Jainism a resilient Indian minority.

**AP as a Buddhist heartland (the crucial state point)**: Andhra was one of India's **greatest Buddhist regions** — **Amaravati** (the Mahachaitya/Great Stupa, Satavahana-era, the 'Amaravati school' of art), **Nagarjunakonda** (Ikshvaku-era; named for **Acharya Nagarjuna**, the Madhyamaka philosopher), **Bhattiprolu** (relic casket, early Brahmi), Salihundam, Guntupalli, Ghantasala — a dense Buddhist landscape; Nagarjuna's **Madhyamaka (Shunyavada)** philosophy was born here.
**Craft**: the Jain-Buddhist comparison table + the councils/canon + the impact + AP's Amaravati-Nagarjunakonda Buddhist eminence.

**Impact**: Pali/Prakrit literature, stupa & cave architecture, universities (Nalanda), and a lasting ethic of non-violence — while Jainism deeply shaped Gujarat/Karnataka trade and art (Shravanabelagola).

sections.heading: The rise of Magadha and the Mauryan Empire

blocks.text: **Magadha** rose from Mahajanapada to empire through geography and ambition: fertile Gangetic soil, **iron mines (Rajgir), elephants, riverine trade (Ganga), and strong capitals (Rajagriha→Pataliputra)**. Its dynasties: **Haryanka (Bimbisara, Ajatashatru), Shishunaga, Nanda (Mahapadma Nanda — the vast wealth-and-army that even Alexander's troops feared)** → overthrown by **Chandragupta Maurya (c. 321 BCE)** with **Chanakya (Kautilya)**, founding the **Mauryan Empire — India's first pan-subcontinental state**.

rows: Founded the empire; defeated Seleucus (treaty — 500 elephants, marriage alliance, **Megasthenes** as envoy); unified most of the subcontinent; late-life Jain ascetic (Shravanabelagola)
'Amitraghata' (slayer of foes); extended into the Deccan; contact with the Hellenistic world
The zenith (HCOI-007); Kalinga war → Dhamma; the edicts
Weak successors, over-centralisation, financial strain, Brahmanical reaction; **Brihadratha killed by Pushyamitra Shunga (185 BCE)** — the Shunga takeover

items: **Administration (the Arthashastra + Megasthenes' Indica)**: a **centralised bureaucratic state** — king at apex with a council (mantriparishad), **provinces (under princes-kumaras) → districts → villages**, an elaborate official hierarchy (**samaharta-revenue, sannidhata-treasury, adhyakshas-superintendents**), **espionage network**, standing army, and land-revenue (~1/4 to 1/6) as the fiscal base — the PA-notes' Kautilyan machinery (PIII-PAG-014) in its historical setting.

**Sources**: **Kautilya's Arthashastra** (statecraft), **Megasthenes' Indica** (the Greek ambassador's account — the seven-caste description, Pataliputra's grandeur, though partly garbled), **Ashokan edicts** (the contemporary royal voice), Buddhist-Jain texts, Visakhadatta's Mudrarakshasa, and archaeology (Northern Black Polished Ware, punch-marked coins).

**Assessment**: the Mauryas achieved unprecedented **political unification, economic integration (currency, trade routes, state farms), and cultural patronage (Buddhism's spread)** — but the over-centralised, tax-heavy, personality-dependent state fragmented after Ashoka; still, it set the template of the pan-Indian empire.

**AP link**: Mauryan authority reached the Andhra region — **Ashokan minor rock edicts at Erragudi/Yerragudi (Kurnool district), Rajula-Mandagiri** — AP was within the empire; the Satavahanas rose from its Deccan feudatories.

sections.heading: Ashoka and Dhamma — conquest to conscience

blocks.text: **Ashoka (r. 268-232 BCE)**, the Mauryan zenith, is history's rare king who **renounced war after victory**. The **Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE — ~1 lakh killed, 1.5 lakh deported, by his own edict's count)** so anguished him that he embraced **Buddhism** and replaced **bherighosha (drum of war) with dhammaghosha (drum of dharma)**. His governing philosophy — **Dhamma** — was NOT Buddhism-as-state-religion but a **universal ethical-social code**: non-violence, tolerance of all sects, respect for elders-teachers-Brahmanas-shramanas, care for servants-animals, truthfulness, and welfare — a moral cement for a diverse empire, propagated through **edicts** and officials (**Dhamma Mahamatras**).

rows: Dhamma principles, welfare, sect-tolerance, animal-welfare; on rocks along the empire's edges
On polished sandstone pillars (the **Sarnath lion capital — India's national emblem**); Dhamma & administration
Personal faith declarations; **Maski & Gujarra name 'Ashoka' explicitly** (confirming identity with 'Devanampiya Piyadasi')
**Brahmi (mostly), Kharosthi (NW), Greek & Aramaic (Afghan edicts — Kandahar)** — Prakrit dialects; deciphered by **James Prinsep (1837)**

sections.heading: Assessing Dhamma — and the AP thread

items: **What Dhamma was and wasn't**: NOT a sectarian imposition (Ashoka explicitly urged respect for ALL sects) but a **civic-moral ethic** aimed at social harmony in a vast, plural empire; scholars debate whether it was genuine spiritual conviction, a pragmatic unifying ideology, or both — present it as ethical-political statecraft, sincerely held.

**Ashoka's contributions**: propagation of Buddhism across Asia (missions — his son **Mahinda & daughter Sanghamitta to Sri Lanka**), the **3rd Buddhist Council**, monumental art (pillars, stupas — enlarged Sanchi), welfare-state measures (hospitals for humans-animals, roads-wells-rest houses, the first 'welfare' governance), and the **edicts as India's first written historical records** in the subcontinent.

**Critical view**: some argue Dhamma's pacifism weakened Mauryan military vigour (contributing to decline) — a debated point; but Ashoka's stature as a moral exemplar of governance is near-universal (H.G. Wells' famous praise; the national emblem-and-Chakra legacy).

**AP thread**: Ashoka's **minor rock edicts at Erragudi/Yerragudi and Rajula-Mandagiri (Kurnool)** proclaimed Dhamma on Andhra soil — 'all men are my children' (savve munisse paja mama) was inscribed here; AP was part of the Dhamma empire.

items: **Similarities**: both centre non-violence, tolerance, ethical conduct and compassion; Dhamma drew its vocabulary from Buddhist and broader Indian ethics.
**Differences**: Buddhism = religion & path to Nirvana (Tripitaka); Dhamma = **public moral policy** for social harmony, with no scripture, propagated by edict and by **Dhamma Mahamatras**.
**Instruments**: Major & Minor Rock Edicts, Pillar Edicts (Brahmi/Prakrit; Kharoshthi & Greek/Aramaic at the frontiers); welfare works — hospitals, wells, rest-houses, roadside trees.
**Legacy**: Ashoka carried Buddhism across Asia (son **Mahinda** & daughter **Sanghamitra** to Sri Lanka), and modelled an early ideal of ethical, tolerant governance.

**Dhamma ≠ Buddhism:** it was a broad civic-moral ethic for a plural empire, not sectarian imposition — the debate on whether it weakened the empire (pacifism) or strengthened social cohesion.
**Andhra connection:** Ashokan minor rock edicts in the south (e.g., **Rajula-Mandagiri, Erragudi in Kurnool region**) show Mauryan reach into Andhra.
**Assessment:** a pioneering experiment in **ethical statecraft and welfare** (roads, wells, hospitals, tolerance) — a favourite Ethics-paper cross-reference too.

**Dhamma Mahamatras** = officers of morality; **3rd Buddhist Council** at Pataliputra (Moggaliputta Tissa) under Ashoka.
Missions: **Mahinda & Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka**; Ashoka titled **Devanampiya Piyadasi**.
Welfare: hospitals for humans & animals, wells, rest-houses, banyan avenues.
mainsAngles: A king who renounced war after winning — analyse Kalinga as the turning point of Ashoka's reign.
Dhamma was civic ethic, not state religion — establish the distinction and its purpose in a plural empire.
The edicts are India's first written history — evaluate them as sources and as governance.
Did Dhamma's pacifism weaken the empire? Assess the debated link to Mauryan decline.
'All men are my children' was proclaimed on Andhra soil — trace Ashokan Dhamma in the AP region.

glossary.definition: Ashoka's universal ethical-social code (non-violence, tolerance, welfare) — civic morality, not sectarian Buddhism.
Ashoka's officials charged with propagating and overseeing Dhamma across the empire.
'Beloved of the Gods, of gracious countenance' — Ashoka's title in the edicts.
Ashoka's bloody conquest of Kalinga (c. 261 BCE) whose carnage triggered his moral transformation.
The Ashokan pillar capital adopted as India's national emblem.
Ashokan minor rock edicts in Kurnool proclaiming Dhamma in the Andhra region.
